We made the argument (and I believe it) that differences in home range size (and hence sigma) should affect g0 (or lambda0 in the HHN parameterization). On the other hand, it is conceivable that g0 might vary independently even when sigma is constant, so (g0~h2, sigma~1) seems meaningful (but not consistent with your observation that sexes differ in home range size, and therefore perhaps not worth considering). The only issue with (g0~h2, sigma~h2) is that it may be more than is needed cf (a0~1, sigma~h2).
Murray

I'll just add my 2 cents here.  Compensation between g0 and sigma based on proportional space use makes sense, but other factors influence g0 and could potentially have a larger influence on g0 differences than space use.  For example, male felids have larger sigmas then females, but in camera trap studies where cameras are placed on larger trails, their g0 may be roughly the same as females because they use the larger trails more extensively.  Sure, it's probably not exactly the same, but g0~1 sigma~h2 may be an efficient way to model this.  I'm sure there are cases where some other behavioral difference between groups can mitigate, outweigh, or add to the effects of differential space use.

messages.body_plain:
I have two cents more. I suspect there might frequently be little or no compensation between g0 and sigma in the case sex-specific sigma for adults.  Males frequently have larger home ranges than females so that their range includes or overlaps the ranges of several reproductive females.  Males then travel extensively within these large ranges, checking on the reproductive status of, and advertising themselves to, several females, and marking or defending their territory to exclude other males. The large male home range is not about meeting energetic requirements, it's about maximizing reproductive output. Females need to devote energy to gestation, lactation, etc, but more of males' energetic investment into reproduction comes in the form of movement. Therefore, at least at some times of year, males may just as likely to be at any specific location within their large range as females would be within a smaller one (hence no compensation between g0 and sigma).

In the case of black bears, males have much larger ranges than females and move extensively within those ranges during the breeding season, but after the breeding season both sexes travel extensively in search of food, and the difference in home range size between sexes decreases or disappears (based on unpublished home data from Ontario). During the breeding season, I would not expect much compensation between g0 and sigma, and after the breeding season, I would expect sigma to be similar between sexes (and the assumption that activity centers are fixed suspect).  I haven't reviewed SECR studies of black bears recently enough to back up these claims with sex-specific estimates of model parameters during and after the breeding season!

Eric

I think this is impossible.  Males can't cover more area without reducing space use in the area already covered.  But since they're moving around their larger home range faster, than females are moving around their smaller home ranges, they may be more likely to be close enough to a trap to smell the bait and be pulled in.  Another consideration is that if you are doing any subsampling of your hair samples, which is common, if larger males deposit more hair samples than smaller females the subsampling process will lower the g0 more for females than males, potentially mitigating or swamping compensation between g0 and sigma from space use.  Or if hair snares are closer to larger trails that the males preferentially use, females with cubs may avoid these areas.

Based on bear GPS data from KY, I agree that females have reduced space use in the spring and early summer compared to fall, but we saw smaller home ranges for females in all seasons.  But as I'm sure you know, hair snare studies are usually done in the spring to early summer when there is less food on the landscape and hair is easier to snag and this is when the difference is most pronounced.  From my vague memory of bear hair snare studies in the literature and one I worked on recently, I think sigma estimates of males are around 2x that of females.  And SCR is pretty robust to mobile activity centers, at least on well-spaced and regular trapping arrays. messages.body_plain:
Hi Elsa

mask.check() tries a model with new masks formed by buffering different distances around the detectors. You can either specify these with the 'buffers' argument or rely on default multiples of the buffer used for the original mask. Unfortunately, the original buffer width is not saved as such and must be inferred from the mask saved with the fitted model. That is where the code is tripping up: it is inferring a near-to-zero original buffer, which is useless (multiples of zero are also zero); recognising this it tells you to specify the buffers argument rather than rely on the automatic default.

You have used the default 100-m buffer in secr.fit. This is too small for leopards. I cannot quite see why 'secr' thinks 100 m is effectively zero - probably because it is less than the mask cell size (spacing). I predict the problem will go away if you specify a more plausible mask (via the buffer argument).

As an aside - I find there are quicker ways to assess buffer adequacy e.g. esa.plot(). See also suggest.buffer() or for halfnormal detection functions just use buffer = 4 * RPSV(CH, CC=TRUE).

Sorry for the slightly delayed response - blame the time zones.
Murray

messages.subject: two step modeling process
messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

I'm interested in using secr to answer questions on how hunting alters black bear spatial parameters, particularly density. I've proposed a two step modeling process 1) identify most parsimonious model for sigma and lambda0 (i.e., D~1); 2) using the most parsimonious model for lambda0 and sigma from step 1, identify most parsimonious model for D using spatial covariates.

I am aware that in some cases, two step modeling approaches sometimes gets different results than a single model run. Running models in two stages, for me, would be a more time efficient means to answering my research questions because secr models have been very time intensive.

Does anyone have any opinions or suggestions as to why a two-step approach for secr models is a bad/good idea?

Thanks in advance,
Annie

messages.subject: Re: two step modeling process
messages.body_plain:
Hi Annie,
I and others have used similar approaches. You could run into some trouble if some of the covariates of detection parameters were similar or the same as those for density. Suppose density but not detection parameters differ by habitat type, and you use habitat type at the trap site as a covariate for detection probability, and also plan to use habitat type as a spatial covariate of density.  In this case, the trap covariate could be strongly supported in step 1 if you assume constant density when fitting models with and without the trap covariate.  When you move to step 2, retaining habitat type as a covariate of detection parameters and also modelling density as a function of habitat type, we would hope that the parameter estimates would reflect the truth, i.e., that density differs but detection parameters are similar between habitat types, but in this case you might not even fit a potentially better model: one where detection parameters are not affected by habitat type at all but density is.  With more data, you can tease these things out, but I usually try to avoid potentially confounded covariates of detection and density.

Cheers,
Eric

I'm very new to the secr package, so please forgive my inexperience. I'm planning on running hundreds of simulations to assess different trap layouts. One of these trap layouts will be a cluster design. cluster <- make.grid(nx = 2, ny = 2,

I hope all of this makes sense? I'd really appreciate some help on this.

Thanks in advance!

Ross

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ross

I think you have reached the limit of what is possible with secr 2.10. Buried in the code for trap.builder there is a note suggesting that future versions should allow a minimum separation, so I guess it's not yet available! Apart from that, I tend to think what you are attempting is rather arcane and likely to result in very slight differences in estimator efficiency. Specifically, the properties of the SECR estimates can probably be determined with a systematic grid of widely-spaced clusters, and cluster rotation probably is not relevant if animals are placed at random. Also, you are aiming to constrain a SRS (simple random sample), but a spatially balanced sample would be better (systematic, GRTS or the recently published Balanced Acceptance Sampling - see package SDraw).

Your solution - containing random clusters within a smaller region to adjust (average) spacing - might work, but is it worth the hassle?

Murray

PS You have rotation = "-", but I think the idea is to use a negative number: rotation = -1.

messages.body_plain:
Mostly, "it's complicated", and I wasn't feeling like definitively laying out the issues :-). The key one (not emphasised in the publications) is that a0 works as a surrogate for effective sampling area a (the quantity that reliably integrates sigma and lambda0) only if the sampling regime is constant (fixed detector locations and duration of sampling).

Seasonal change in home range overlap implies seasonal change in the parameter k (which appears in the software as sigmak). In principle you can compare seasonal and constant models for sigmak. However, in your case density is not likely to vary much seasonally (so would not drive variation in sigma through constant k), and a model with seasonal k may be exactly equivalent to a model with seasonal sigma. Whether 'a0 models' are appropriate is a separate issue - that concerns how variation in sigma drives variation in lambda0.

Murray
